source.title: Rethinking Deep Alignment Through The Lens Of Incomplete Learning
source.authors: Thong Bach; Dung Nguyen; T. Le; Truyen Tran

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures position-wise distributional differences and adversarial safety behavior, and proposes a different method for detecting and completing shallow alignment. It is a conceptual test and extension rather than a replication of the original interventions.
record.gate_note: The paper's argument about gradient weakening is presented as a mechanism, but it does not report measured per-position gradient magnitudes. Its post-training token-frequency analysis is described inconsistently: the text says base-favored token frequencies increase after an intervention intended to suppress them; those frequencies are not treated as evidence of the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own measurements of several versions on four Llama and Qwen chat models. These are position-wise aligned-vs-base KL on harmful prompts (V3), prefill and GCG attack success on standard aligned models (V4), and harmful-rate rises after benign Dolly LoRA fine-tuning against a pre-fine-tuning reference in Table 4 (V2). It also tests whether a deepening method holds up under prefill, GCG and fine-tuning, alongside a re-run of the original Safety Augmentation method (V7). The methods differ from the originals: a new completion loss, human-judged ASR and an AdvBench subset.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors argue that position-dependent gradient weakening in autoregressive training leaves safety learning incomplete in later positions. They propose base-favored tokens as detectors of this and a targeted completion method (L2 penalties plus hybrid-teacher distillation). They report 48–98% lower attack success, recovery of safety after benign fine-tuning (HRR 0.3–1.0) with utility preserved, and more safety deliberation in Qwen-3.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce harmful-example fine-tuning or the original benign-fine-tuning intervention. It measures position-wise aligned/base KL and attacks, then tests a targeted completion and contrastive decoding method.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary by model: baseline prefill attack success ranges from 23.0% to 96.1%, and targeted completion leaves rates from 0.5% to 44.3%.

fits_no_version.finding: Inference-time contrastive decoding that penalizes base-favored tokens raises aligned-vs-base KL throughout the response (about 10→6). It cuts 4-token prefill ASR from 47.5% to 0.2% with small utility change.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An inference-time decoding defense that pushes the distribution away from the base model at every position removes prefill vulnerability.

record.problems: The gradient-decay mechanism is argued rather than empirically measured. The positional KL analyses are mostly described in figures and lack a numerical per-position table. Table 3 does not provide matched pre-fine-tuning safety scores, and the fine-tuning HRR label/value direction is not reconciled with the text's descriptions. The reported base-favored token frequency change after completion is described inconsistently with the stated suppression objective.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Table 4 reports safety-recovery and utility comparisons after benign fine-tuning; those recovery-method comparisons are not separately cataloged because the relevant direct fine-tuning robustness outcomes are already represented in Table 3. The paper's reasoning-engagement and utility benchmark results do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: No localization or editing of weights or ranks.
The gradient-concentration mechanism is argued but never measured. There is no comparison of data or objectives.
Decoding changes as a bypass are not tested; only prefill and GCG are.
The trained model's per-position KL profile is not measured, so whether training spreads divergence beyond the first tokens is unshown. KL spread is shown only for contrastive decoding.
No numeric per-position table. Concentration in the first few positions versus gradual decay cannot be quantified.

missing.what: Pre- and post-fine-tuning harmful rates (Base vs LoRA): Llama-3.1 1.4→25.5, Qwen-2.5 0.0→24.7, Llama-2 0.0→21.4. These are the matched baselines for V2.
Prefill ASR rises from 47.4% (uncompromised model) to 78.4% after LoRA fine-tuning. The model is not clearly stated.
Qi et al. Safety Augmentation re-run on Llama-2-7B-Chat: prefill 0.8%, GCG 1.6%±3.6, fine-tuning HRR 4.4.
Prefill ASR after recovery: targeted completion 44.5%, Vaccine 71.9%, SaLoRA 69.3%, Safe LoRA 73.4%.

record.verdict_notes: 'Harmfulness Rejection Rate' is marked lower-is-better, so it is read as a harmful-output rate; the name is contradictory. ASR is judged by human evaluators on 384 AdvBench prompts. The Figure 5 caption says increased base-favored token frequencies show suppression, which is internally inconsistent. The 'Base' label in Table 4 and Figure 4 seems to mean the uncompromised aligned model, not the pretrained model. GCG variance at baseline is very large (±42.9). The gradient mechanism for V6 is an argument, not a result, so no V6 verdict is given.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment fine-tunes a safety-trained model on harmful examples and measures whether that makes it comply.
The reported results do not give a matched pre-fine-tuning safety measure for the same models and evaluation set.

The paper reports declining positional KL, but does not provide a numerical per-position KL table or a quantitative test of whether the decline is concentrated in the first few positions versus spread evenly.
The paper tests prefill and GCG suffix attacks. It does not test decoding changes as a way to bypass safety; its contrastive decoding experiment is a defense.
No experiment identifies or edits a small set of weights or ranks carrying safety behavior.
The proposed gradient explanation is argued analytically, not tested by measuring training gradients or comparing training objectives.
The paper reports attack robustness after its completion training, but does not directly measure whether training spreads the aligned-versus-base KL profile beyond the first response tokens.
